sandhi.note: ā + e → ai; the final m becomes anusvāra before त्वम् (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).
Final n before t becomes ṃs (पुमांस्तिष्ठेत्); the t of तिष्ठेत् becomes d before the vowel of अग्रे.

morph.note: Imperative of √ब्रू with the ending -हि. After मा, Pāṇinian Sanskrit uses the aorist without augment (मा वोचः); मा with the imperative is the looser usage of the epics and Purāṇas, with the same prohibitive sense.
Optative of √स्था (present stem तिष्ठ-): ‘could, would stand’. In a rhetorical question it means ‘no one could’.
Nominative singular of the irregular stem पुंस् ‘man’: पुमान्, पुमांसौ, पुमांसः.

mantras.anvaya: देवि, त्वम् अवलिप्ता असि; मम अग्रतः एवं मा ब्रूहि। त्रैलोक्ये कः पुमान् शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः अग्रे तिष्ठेत्?
mantras.anvaya_en: A statement, a prohibition (मा … ब्रूहि), and a rhetorical question with the optative.
mantras.lit: You are arrogant, O Devī; do not speak thus in front of me. In the three worlds what man could stand before Śumbha and Niśumbha?
mantras.tr: You are proud, O Devī. Do not speak so in my presence. What man in the three worlds could stand before Śumbha and Niśumbha?

comm.t: The messenger takes the vow as arrogance (अवलिप्ता) and rejects it: no man in the three worlds can face the two brothers, so a contest is absurd.

The word दर्प ‘pride’ of the vow (5.120) is answered with अवलिप्ता ‘puffed up’. The irony runs the other way in the narrative: it is the asuras’ pride that will be removed, in the battles of chapters 6–10. Śumbha himself will make the same charge at the end, बलावलेपात् ‘from pride in strength’ (10.3).

morph.note: एक ‘one’ with the suffix -क (here diminishing or contemptuous: ‘a mere lone …’); the feminine turns the a before क to i (एकिका). It mocks the Devī for standing without an army.
In the idiom किं पुनः, ‘what again …?’ means ‘how much less (or more)’: an argument from the greater to the lesser.
Locative singular of the root-noun युध् ‘battle’ (feminine): युध् + इ.

mantras.anvaya: देवि, सर्वे देवाः अन्येषाम् अपि दैत्यानां सम्मुखे युधि न वै तिष्ठन्ति; एकिका स्त्री त्वं किं पुनः?
mantras.anvaya_en: A negative statement followed by the elliptical rhetorical question किं पुनः (‘how much less [will] you …’), whose verb is understood from तिष्ठन्ति.
mantras.lit: All the gods do not indeed stand in battle face to face even with other Daityas, O Devī — how much less you, a woman, alone?
mantras.tr: Not all the gods together can stand in battle even before the lesser Daityas, O Devī — how much less you, a woman, alone!
mantras.tr_note: अन्येषाम् ‘other’ is rendered ‘lesser’ to bring out the contrast with Śumbha and Niśumbha.

comm.t: The messenger argues from the greater to the lesser: the gods cannot face even the other Daityas; a lone woman cannot face the brothers.

Being alone and a woman is, for the messenger, the decisive weakness. The narrative will turn both against the asuras: Śumbha will taunt her for relying on other goddesses, and she will withdraw them all into herself to fight alone (10.3–6).

samasa.literal: those of whom Indra is the first
of those of whom Śumbha is the first

morph.note: Perfect third plural of √स्था: reduplicated त- + स्थ् + -उः, the root vowel lost before the ending. ‘Stood (firm)’, i.e. held their ground.
Simple future of प्र + √या (या + स्य): ‘will you go’. With कथम्: ‘how will you (dare to) go?’.
Nominative singular of the irregular feminine स्त्री, the subject being ‘you’ implied by the verb: ‘(you,) a woman’.

mantras.anvaya: येषां (सम्मुखे) संयुगे इन्द्राद्याः सकलाः देवाः न तस्थुः, तेषां शुम्भादीनां सम्मुखं (त्वं) स्त्री कथं प्रयास्यसि?
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (येषां … न तस्थुः) names the asuras; the main clause is a rhetorical question with the future प्रयास्यसि, its subject ‘you’ implied.
mantras.lit: Of whom in battle all the gods headed by Indra did not stand (before) — how will you, a woman, go to the front of those, Śumbha and the rest?
mantras.tr: Indra and all the gods could not hold their ground in battle against Śumbha and his host. How will you, a woman, go out to face them?
mantras.tr_note: The relative construction is turned into two sentences.

comm.t: The messenger repeats his argument with a fact the hearer knows: Indra and all the gods were defeated by these asuras (5.2–5). How then can a woman go out against them?

The listener has just heard the same defeated gods praise the Devī as the power behind all beings (5.9–82). The messenger’s reasoning measures her against the gods; the text has already placed her above them.

samasa.vigraha: केशानाम् आकर्षणम् केशाकर्षणम्; केशाकर्षणेन निर्धूतं गौरवं यस्याः सा
samasa.type: bahuvrīhi containing a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa (केशाकर्षणनिर्धूत) and a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (केशाकर्षण)
samasa.literal: she whose dignity has been shaken off by the dragging of the hair
samasa.sense: dragged by the hair and stripped of all honour

morph.note: Future of √गम् (गम् + इष्य). With मा it expresses a warning: ‘do not (end up) going …’, ‘lest you go …’. Pāṇini’s prohibitive construction is मा with the unaugmented aorist; मा with the future is a looser epic and Purāṇic usage.
Past participle of √वच्: ‘(you) having been told by me alone’ — that is, go now at a messenger’s word, while it is still a request.

mantras.anvaya: सा त्वं मया एव उक्ता (सती) शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः पार्श्वं गच्छ; केशाकर्षणनिर्धूतगौरवा (सती) मा गमिष्यसि।
mantras.anvaya_en: An imperative (गच्छ) and a prohibitive future (मा गमिष्यसि) set against each other: go now willingly, not later by force.
mantras.lit: So go, bidden by me alone, to the side of Śumbha and Niśumbha; do not go (later) with your dignity shaken off by the dragging of your hair.
mantras.tr: Go, then, to Śumbha and Niśumbha now, at my word alone — lest you go dragged there by the hair, stripped of your honour.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Now’ and ‘later’ (lit.) and ‘lest’ (tr) bring out the contrast of the two verbs; they are implied, not stated.

comm.t: The messenger ends with a threat: let her go willingly at his word, or she will be taken by force, dragged by the hair. The threat sets up the next chapter, where Dhūmralocana is sent to do exactly that (6.3–4: केशाकर्षणविह्वलाम्).

Dragging by the hair is the extreme insult to a woman’s honour in the epic world. The threat turns back on those who make it: the asuras sent to seize her are destroyed, beginning with Dhūmralocana in the next chapter.
